name: 10K Race Plan
subtitle: Jul 6 -- Oct 3, 2026 · 13 weeks · 3 runs/wk → 4 runs/wk → 10K race

phases.name: Rebuild
phases.description: Re-establish a running base on your recovering soleus. Three runs with strides on Monday and Thursday to start building turnover speed. Keep base pace at 9:30-10:00/mi. Sunday is always rest.

phases.name: Rebuild
phases.description: Same frequency, shorter distances. Let your body absorb the work from the last three weeks.

phases.name: Build
phases.description: Add a short post-squat shakeout on Wednesday before bench. Thursday is the speed day: hill repeats build power with less impact than flat intervals. Long run grows to 6.5 miles. From week 7 the week flips: long run opens Monday on two days of rest, Friday becomes the speed day, and strides move to Wednesday.

phases.name: Build
phases.description: Same frequency, shorter distances. Let your body absorb the work from the last three weeks.

phases.name: Peak
phases.description: Monday long run peaks at 7.5 miles in week 11. Friday shifts from hills to race-pace tempo, four clear days after the long run. Wednesday carries strides before bench; Saturday's shakeout before deadlift flushes Friday's tempo. Fewer, better-spaced runs: every quality session gets at least two days of fresh legs in front of it.

phases.name: Taper
phases.description: Cut volume 30-40% but keep the same frequency. Short strides keep your legs sharp without accumulating fatigue. Reduce squat/deadlift weight by ~30% this week. Saturday's short run doubles as a race-morning rehearsal: run it at the same clock time the race starts.

phases.name: Race week
phases.description: Minimal running. The work is done. Keep moving to stay loose, but nothing that leaves you tired. Skip deadlift... the race replaces it. Target pace: ~8:30/mi (52-53 min).

afterPlan.name: After the race
afterPlan.description: Take 3-4 easy days, then resume at the week 9-12 pattern as a repeating cycle: three build weeks, one recovery week. Grow the long run to 8 miles; grow midweek runs by 0.5 mi per cycle. Cap around 22-25 mi/week.

glossary.definition: 9:30-10:00/mi, conversational pace. You should be able to talk in full sentences.
Slightly slower than easy (9:45-10:15/mi). The distance is the workout, not the speed.
After the run, do 4 x 20-sec smooth accelerations to ~90% speed, with a full walk-back recovery between each.
Hill repeats: 1 mi warmup, 6-8 x 30-sec hard uphill, jog down to recover, 1 mi cooldown.
1 mi easy warmup, 2 mi at race pace (~8:30/mi), 1 mi easy cooldown. "Comfortably hard."
Shakeout: a very short, very easy jog just to keep your legs loose. Should feel almost too easy.
Short easy run before that day's lift. The run comes first.
Deadlift day. "lt" means light: reduce working weight ~30%.
Reduce barbell weight ~30% from normal working sets. Keep the movement, cut the load.
Amber-highlighted weeks. Same frequency, shorter runs. Where adaptation actually happens.

rules.label: Pace
rules.text: Every run except the long run: 9:30-10:00/mi. Conversational. If you can't talk in full sentences, slow down. The long run: 9:45-10:15/mi, even slower.

rules.label: Shakeouts
rules.text: The 2-mile runs are recovery, not training. They should feel almost pointlessly easy. If your legs feel heavy from yesterday's squats, that's expected... run through it gently.

rules.label: Recovery wks
rules.text: Every 4th week, drop volume ~25%. Keep the same frequency but shorten every run. These weeks are where adaptation happens... don't skip them.

rules.label: Soleus
rules.text: Add bent-knee calf raises to your squat day (you're already on the smith machine). 3 sets of 15, slow 3-second lowering. Also do a bodyweight set of 20 before every run as part of your warmup.

rules.label: Squat day
rules.text: Never run the same day as squat day. Your squat session (barbell squat, machine squat, standing calf raises) is the heaviest leg stimulus in your week. It gets a buffer on both sides. Bench and deadlift pair fine with short runs.

rules.label: Long run
rules.text: From week 7 the long run opens the week on Monday, coming off Sunday rest and a Saturday shakeout... two clear days of fresh legs. 18 months of your own data show runs on 1 day of rest cost ~7% efficiency, and your best long runs all came on 2-3 days of rest; sleep quality doesn't rescue a back-to-back day. Tuesday squat after the long run is fine: lifts the day before or after a run show no penalty in your history. Sunday is always off.

rules.label: Strides
rules.text: After Monday and Thursday runs in weeks 1-3: 4x20 seconds at fast-but-relaxed effort with full recovery walk between. Not sprinting -- smooth, quick turnover. These are free speed with almost zero injury risk. Drop them on recovery weeks.

rules.label: Hill repeats
rules.text: Weeks 5-7 (Thursday through week 6, Friday from week 7): find a moderate hill (4-6% grade). 1 mi warmup, 6x30 sec hard uphill, jog down recovery, 1 mi cooldown. Hills build power and teach your body to use less energy at faster speeds, with less joint impact than flat intervals. Grow to 8 reps by week 7.

rules.label: Tempo runs
rules.text: Friday in weeks 9-11, four days after the long run and off a Thursday rest: 1 mile easy warmup, 2 miles at ~8:30/mi (10K race pace), 1 mile easy cooldown. This teaches sustained effort. It should feel "comfortably hard" -- you can talk in short phrases but not sentences.

rules.label: 10K target
rules.text: Based on your predicted 5K of 25:07, a realistic 10K goal is ~52-53 minutes (~8:25-8:35/mi). Start conservative: run the first 2 miles at 8:40, settle into 8:30 for miles 3-5, and push the last mile. Don't go out fast.

rules.label: Bail signals
rules.text: Sharp pain in the soleus at any point: stop, walk home, drop back one phase for a week. Dull ache that fades within the first mile: fine, continue. Ache that gets worse as you run: stop.

callout: **The hardest part of this plan is running slowly.** Your natural easy pace is ~9:15/mi, which puts you in Zone 3 (148-161 bpm) -- too hard for base building. Truly easy running means Zone 2 (119-147 bpm): it builds your aerobic capacity without accumulating tissue stress. The volume increase only works if the intensity stays low. Speed comes later... after you own the volume.
